threads_text: Meta is selling up to $95 billion of stock to pay for AI, starting with about $35 billion today. Nvidia, AMD and Broadcom have told Meta they may buy up to $5 billion of it at the same price as everyone else. Would you put your own money into an AI buildout this big?
caption:
Meta said Monday it plans to raise up to $95 billion by selling stock to fund its AI buildout.
About $35 billion is being sold now, and a $60 billion program of non voting Class C shares could start in early 2027.
Nvidia, AMD and Broadcom have signaled non binding interest in up to $5 billion of the shares.
Meta expects to spend $135 billion to $145 billion on capital projects this year.

Would you buy into an AI buildout this expensive?

site_article.headline: Meta plans to raise up to $95 billion in stock to fund its AI buildout
site_article.dek: Nvidia, AMD and Broadcom have signaled non binding interest in up to $5 billion of the first tranche.
site_article.summary: Meta said on October 26, 2026 that it will sell about $35 billion of stock now and may sell up to $60 billion more through a later program, for a total of about $95 billion. The money is for artificial intelligence infrastructure.
site_article.seo_title: Meta plans up to $95 billion stock sale to fund AI
site_article.seo_description: Meta said on October 26, 2026 it will sell about $35 billion of stock now and up to $60 billion more later to fund AI infrastructure.
site_article.answer_summary: Meta is raising up to about $95 billion in equity to pay for AI data centers and computing power. About $35 billion is being sold now, and a $60 billion at the market program of non voting Class C shares could begin in the first quarter of 2027.
site_article.hero_alt: The entrance sign at Meta's Menlo Park campus, showing the company logo beside a road.

paragraphs.text: Meta Platforms said on October 26, 2026 that it plans to raise up to about $95 billion by selling stock, and that the money will go toward the computing power behind its artificial intelligence work. The company launched two concurrent underwritten offerings worth roughly $35 billion the same day, according to Benzinga and a filing Meta made with the Securities and Exchange Commission.

The first tranche has two parts. One is about $22.5 billion of Class A common stock sold through forward sale agreements, initially with Morgan Stanley Capital Services and Goldman Sachs, which Meta can settle on dates it chooses up to November 19, 2027. The other is 250 million depositary shares, worth about $12.5 billion, each representing a 1/20th interest in a share of Series A mandatory convertible preferred stock with a $1,000 liquidation preference. The depositary shares are intended to trade on Nasdaq under the symbol METAM and to convert into common stock around August 15, 2029.

Because the common stock is being sold through forward sale agreements, Meta said it does not expect to receive those proceeds immediately. Morgan Stanley and Goldman Sachs are the lead joint bookrunning managers for both offerings, and the completion of one is not conditioned on the completion of the other, according to the filing. Meta said the proceeds are for general corporate purposes.

Nvidia, Advanced Micro Devices and Broadcom have indicated interest in buying up to $5 billion of the Class A stock in total, on the same terms as other buyers and with no discount, the filing said. Those indications are not binding, and the three companies may buy more, less or none of the shares. All three sell chips or networking parts used in the data centers Meta is building.

The larger part of the plan has not started. Meta said it intends to set up an at the market program of up to $60 billion that would sell its planned Class C common stock over time, and that the program could begin in the first quarter of 2027, once the Class C shares start trading. Meta has not finalized the terms and has not entered into an agreement, Benzinga reported. The Class C stock was created through an amended certificate of incorporation filed on October 21, 2026, and it carries no votes, which means selling it does not reduce the voting power Mark Zuckerberg holds, according to Business Model Analyst.

The structure is the point. Meta is raising money in a way that converts its share count, rather than its control, into computing power. The forward sales delay the cash, the preferred shares delay the dilution to 2029, and the biggest piece of all is reserved for shares that cannot vote. For investors, that trades governance for access to the buildout.

Meta has guided to capital expenditures of $135 billion to $145 billion for 2026 and says it funds that spending through operating cash flow, debt, partnerships and equity. The company generated about $97 billion in operating cash flow in the first nine months of 2026 and ended September with roughly $82 billion in cash, cash equivalents and marketable securities, Benzinga reported. Third quarter revenue rose 26 percent from a year earlier to $64.6 billion, with net income of $9.9 billion.

Meta says it owns data centers in 23 American states, is building four AI superclusters of more than 1 gigawatt each, and expects to nearly double its total infrastructure capacity in 2026 compared with 2025, according to TipRanks. Meta shares closed at $642.62 on Friday and traded around $635 in premarket dealing on Monday, down about 1 percent, FinanceFeeds reported.

The next marker is whether Nvidia, AMD and Broadcom actually buy, and at what size, when the first tranche prices. After that, watch for the Class C shares to begin trading and for Meta to confirm the terms of the $60 billion program, which would show how much of the buildout the company expects public investors to fund.
